## 2026-02-24 — MCP SEP-1686: Tasks — Call-Now, Fetch-Later Execution (Final)
- **Why it matters:** Solves a fundamental reliability gap in MCP: if a long-running tool call is dropped, clients have no way to query its status or retrieve its result. Without Tasks, agents must re-invoke tools from scratch. This is directly relevant for any MCP tool that takes minutes (CI/CD pipelines, Step Functions, Workflow APIs).
- **Connects to:** Agent reliability (Wink, Gecko), long-horizon task execution, our own tool invocations that might take >seconds. If we're calling any long-running external tools via MCP, this is the right pattern.
## 2026-02-24 — MCP SEP-1577: Sampling With Tools — MCP Servers Running Their Own Agent Loops (Final)
- **Why it matters:** Allows MCP **servers** to invoke the client's LLM with tool-calling enabled, running full agentic loops *using the client's tokens*. This inverts the typical flow: not just "client calls server tools," but "server uses client's LLM to do agentic work." Fundamentally changes what MCP servers can be.
- **Key insight:** Adds `tools` and `toolChoice` params to `sampling/createMessage`. MCP servers can now request LLM completions with tool-call support — enabling servers to run their own reasoning+tool loops. Use case: a complex data-processing MCP server that needs to make multiple decisions before returning a result. The "(still under user supervision)" note is important — user consent flows through the client. Note: `includeContext` is soft-deprecated (its semantics were ambiguous). Low prior adoption (sampling wasn't widely used) — this SEP should unlock it.
- **Connects to:** MCP ecosystem growth (MCP is becoming a full compute substrate, not just a tool-definition layer), agent security (more complex trust boundaries when servers run agent loops), A2A protocol.
## 2026-02-24 — MCP SEP-1865: MCP Apps — Interactive UIs Delivered by MCP Servers (Final)
- **Why it matters:** MCP servers can now deliver **interactive HTML UIs** to hosts via a `ui://` URI scheme. Bi-directional communication between UI and host over JSON-RPC. Adopted by Postman, HuggingFace, Shopify, Goose, ElevenLabs. OpenAI's Apps SDK (Nov 2025) validated the same demand. This is MCP becoming an application distribution platform.
- **Key insight:** `text/html;profile=mcp-app` resource type with `ui://` URIs. Bi-directional comms via MCP's existing JSON-RPC base protocol. Community has been building on `mcpui.dev` as playground. Major adopters already in production. The pattern: an MCP server can expose both tools *and* an interactive UI for those tools — the host renders the UI, the UI calls back to the MCP server, the server calls the LLM. This collapses the tool-provider/UI-provider/LLM-orchestrator into one deployable unit.
- **Connects to:** MCP platform evolution, agent UI patterns, OpenAI Apps SDK convergence. MCP is now: Tools + Resources + Prompts + Tasks + Sampling + Apps. It's a full application runtime.
- **Key insight:** Three decisions made, each notable: (1) **Memory as files** — represent all memory as a set of files in a virtual filesystem backed by Postgres. The insight: "models are good at using filesystems." No specialized memory tools needed — just filesystem read/write. (2) **COALA taxonomy** — memory split into Procedural (rules/behavior → AGENTS.md), Semantic (world facts → arbitrary files), Episodic (past behavior → also files). (3) **Virtual filesystem** — files are stored in Postgres but exposed to the agent as a filesystem. Pluggable backends (S3, MySQL, etc). The "hot path" write pattern: agents edit their memory files *while working*, not just at session end. Also uses industry standards: AGENTS.md for core instructions, `agent skills` format (agentskills.io) for specialized tasks, sub-agent format similar to Claude Code, custom `tools.json` (not mcp.json) to give agents only a *subset* of MCP tools to avoid context overflow.
- **Connects to:** Memory architecture (Theme 2), our own AGENTS.md + memory file approach, TierMem/StateLM, MCP tool subsetting to avoid context overflow. The "memory as filesystem" pattern is directly analogous to what we do with `.openclaw/` directories.
## 2026-02-24 — MCP SEP-1024: Security Requirements for Local Server Installation (MCP Governance)
- **Why it matters:** The MCP governance process has already identified and formally addressed the "one-click MCP server installation" attack vector. This is the protocol-level security response to the supply chain attacks identified in Skill-Inject and Overthinking Loops.
- **Key insight:** Four attack vectors addressed: (1) **Silent Command Execution** — clients auto-execute embedded commands without user consent; (2) **Lack of Visibility** — users can't see what commands run; (3) **Social Engineering** — users trained to trust "MCP server" installs; (4) **Arbitrary Code Execution** — malicious commands in MCP configs distributed via legit channels. The SEP mandates: explicit consent dialogs showing the *exact untruncated command* before execution, affirmative user action required, cancel option. VS Code and Cursor already implement this. Status: **Final** — meaning it's accepted and normative. MCP current version: **2025-11-25**. Active SEP pipeline includes: SEP-1577 (Sampling With Tools), SEP-1686 (Tasks), SEP-1865 (MCP Apps), SEP-1046 (OAuth client credentials), SEP-1024 (Local server security — Final).
- **Connects to:** MCP security cluster (Zombie Agents, Skill-Inject, Overthinking Loops, SMCP, MCPShield). This is the institutional response — the protocol itself is being hardened. The Tasks SEP (1686) and MCP Apps SEP (1865) suggest MCP is growing far beyond tool-calling into a full application platform.
- **Connects to:** Directly relevant to MCP server trust. Any MCP tool we load from a third-party is a potential skill-inject vector. We need authorization frameworks, not just prompt-level filtering.
- **Why it matters:** Identifies and names a fundamental problem: agents in 1M+ token codebases consistently fail to find the *right* files not because of context limits, but because navigation and retrieval are fundamentally different problems. Graph-based navigation via MCP achieves 99.4% success vs 76.2% for vanilla agents.
- **Key insight:** The **Navigation Paradox**: more context doesn't help when the problem is structural navigation (following dependency graphs) rather than semantic search (finding lexically similar code). CodeCompass exposes dependency graphs via an MCP server — agents that use it jump from 76.2% to 99.4% on hidden-dependency tasks. However: 58% of trials with graph access made **zero tool calls** — agents defaulted to lexical search even with graph tools available. The fix: explicit prompt engineering to guide tool adoption. Key distinction: (1) semantic-search tasks — BM25/embedding retrieval wins; (2) structural navigation — graph traversal wins; (3) hidden-dependency tasks — only graph works.
